title: Five smooth stones (1 Samuel 17)
hook: a shepherd refuses the king's armor and faces a giant

segments.voice: Yesterday, the youngest, called in from the sheep and anointed among his brothers. Your line was the lord looks at the heart. Whose heart did you look at? Day four hundred one.

Two armies face each other across a valley, one on each hillside, and for forty days nobody moves. Every morning and every evening, a champion walks out from the Philistine side and shouts across: send me one man. If he beats me, we'll serve you. Goliath of Gath. Huge, in a bronze helmet and a coat of mail, with a spear like a weaver's beam. And every morning, Israel's army, King Saul included, stays put and is afraid. Then Jesse's youngest son shows up from Bethlehem with grain and loaves for his older brothers. He hears the shouting and asks: who is this, to defy the armies of the living God?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE VALLEY.` → `FORTY DAYS OF SHOUTING.` → `A BOY BRINGS BREAD TO HIS BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: David is brought to Saul and offers to fight. Saul says what anyone would: you're a boy, and he's been a warrior since his youth. David answers with his résumé: I keep my father's sheep. When a lion or a bear took a lamb, I went after it. The Lord who saved me from the lion will save me from this Philistine. So Saul says go, and does the generous, sensible thing. He dresses David in his own armor: a bronze helmet, a coat of mail, the king's sword. David tries to walk in it. He clanks a few steps. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I cannot go thus, for I am not used to it." He takes it all off. Then the text slows down to show what he picks up instead: his staff, a sling, and "five smooth stones out of the brook," dropped into his shepherd's bag. Tools he knows. Goliath sees a young man with a stick and is insulted: am I a dog? David's answer is the center of the story: "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts." One stone, slung, and the giant falls on his face. Two things are true here. The story is about trust: the battle is the Lord's, David says, not won by sword and spear. And it's about being yourself: David doesn't win by becoming a smaller copy of Saul. Saul's armor was a gift, kindly meant. It just wasn't his. He fought as a shepherd, with a shepherd's things, and that was enough.
screen: `YOU'RE ONLY A BOY.` · `THE KING'S ARMOR DOESN'T FIT.` · `A STAFF, A SLING, FIVE STONES.` · `IN THE NAME OF THE LORD OF HOSTS.` · then, large: `I CANNOT GO THUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use your own tools. Settle, and breathe. Think of something hard in front of you this week, your own giant. Now notice whose armor you've been trying to wear for it. A boss's style. A parent's way of handling conflict. Someone online who seems to have it all figured out. Picture taking that armor off, piece by piece. Then look in your own bag. What are your five smooth stones? Patience, humor, a skill you practiced alone for years, a friend you trust. Name them. If you pray, you can bring your giant to God. The bell holds the time.
Five smooth stones. What David chose from the brook instead of the king's armor: a shepherd's tools, carried in the name of the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: not in borrowed armor. Today, face one hard thing your own way, with the tools you already know. Day four hundred one.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of David and Goliath in the weekday Mass readings, and Catholic schools and youth programs tell it as a story of trusting God and using the gifts you've been given.

original.note: Hebrew: stone. David chooses five smooth stones from the stream for his shepherd's bag.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tiny boy beats a giant by luck.
what it means: a shepherd refuses the king's borrowed armor, fights with the tools he knows, and trusts that the battle is the Lord's.
what a scholar hears: the chapter states its own point in David's words before the stone flies: the battle is the Lord's, and he saves not with sword and spear.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the Goliath-height manuscript myth item and trapdoor line (manuscript claims are not in the cited text), replaced with 17:47 'the battle is the Lord's'; 'teenager' (no age in the text) made 'Jesse's youngest son'; 'bread and cheese for his brothers' corrected (the cheeses were for the captain, 17:17–18); 'many Catholic schools' softened.
Goliath's height: Masoretic text six cubits and a span (17:4); Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus) and 4QSam(a) four cubits and a span. Feet conversions are approximate; confirm.
'Forty days' (17:16), 'bread and cheese' (17:17–18: parched corn, loaves, and cheeses), and 'spear like a weaver's beam' (17:7) are paraphrased; confirm.
Saul's armor in the Douay: helmet of brass, coat of mail, and David girds the sword (17:38–39).
'Teenager' for David is an inference from 'boy' / 'young man'; the text gives no age.
